claims.text: The damaged component is a high-performance high-entropy alloy, exemplified by equiatomic Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20.
The component contains microstructural discontinuities and regions prone to hot cracking following prior thermal exposure.
Friction stir processing with a non-consumable advanced-material tool can locally rework and repair the damaged zone.
Polycrystalline cubic boron nitride is a suitable example of an advanced tool material for this repair.
The repair should be conducted in an inert atmosphere at 0.4–0.6 Tm with controlled tool traverse and rotation speeds.
Real-time process monitoring can ensure uniform shear and avoid oxidation.
Severe plastic deformation during friction stir processing induces dynamic recrystallization.
Dynamic recrystallization produces a refined and homogenized repair-zone microstructure.
Friction stir processing forms a graded, well-bonded interface between the repair zone and the base material.
Friction stir processing mechanically mixes and reworks the damaged material without melting.
Avoiding a prolonged liquid phase mitigates hot cracking.
Dynamic recrystallization heals microstructural defects and reduces residual stresses.
The friction-stir-repaired region will be crack-free and have enhanced ductility and strength.
The friction-stir-repaired region will resist thermal cycling and mechanical loading better than a traditional fusion-weld repair.
Traditional fusion-weld repairs are prone to hot cracking because of extensive liquid-phase exposure and high thermal gradients.
The friction-stir repair is expected to perform at temperatures up to 0.6 Tm under rapid thermal cycling and high-performance mechanical loads.
Repair-zone refinement may be nonuniform over complex geometries, and long-term cyclic thermomechanical performance remains uncertain.
